posts.content:
As agents move from answering questions to taking action across browsers, code repositories, terminals, and production systems, the security model changes and a successful human login is no longer enough. Organizations need to know which agent is acting, who delegated its authority, what it is allowed to do, and whether they can reconstruct what happened afterward.

That is why we signed the OpenAI open letter on collective cyber defense. No single company can solve this problem alone. 

At 1Password, this work spans our integrations with OpenAI, Codex, Anthropic Claude Code, Cursor, Kiro, Perplexity, and Amazon Web Services (AWS) Secrets Manager, as well as products such as Credential Broker. Each of these efforts is built on the same foundation:

🔷 Verify who or what is making the request
🔷 Bind authority to a specific task
🔷 Deliver access only when it is needed without exposing raw credentials to the model or its context
🔷 Revoke access when the work is complete
🔷 Preserve an evidence trail for consequential actions

Agents should not inherit a person’s entire identity. They need an identity of their own, with explicit scope, limited lifetime, and accountable access.

Security is not the brake on AI adoption. It is the infrastructure that makes responsible adoption possible.

posts.content:
The unlock for agents will not come from trusting the model. It will come from building a system that understands what “done” means and improves its ability to verify it.

Imagine asking an agent to write release notes across 1,247 commits. It returns a polished draft, but the comparison API paginated at 1,000 commits and the agent never followed the cursor. The result looks complete even though 247 commits never entered the context.

At 1Password, we separate two questions that are often conflated in agent security:

1/ Was the agent allowed to take the path it took? This is the domain of identity, scoped tools, mediated access, and continuous authorization. These controls limit the blast radius, but they do not prove that the work was completed correctly.

2/ Does the agent's work tie out? This requires what we think of as parity bits for goals: inexpensive, independent, deterministic facts that must be true if the work is complete.

These checks do not prove that the release notes are well written. They establish something more fundamental: that the agent received the complete inputs and produced an internally consistent result.

Good PMs, engineers, and operators already carry these checks in their heads. Accountants call them control totals. We are making that verification instinct executable and reusable.

Before a new kind of task runs, a separate model drafts its measurable acceptance checks. A human reviews and ratifies them once, and the harness stores the resulting deterministic verifier against a strict task signature defined by its inputs, tools, output type, and side effects.

When the same task shape appears again, the harness runs the approved verifier automatically. When the task shape, tool, source schema, or policy changes, the verifier returns for review. The executor never writes its own checks, evaluates its own compliance, or decides that a previously approved verifier is close enough.

The verification also follows the decomposition of the goal. Each subtask receives its own parity checks, and its postconditions become the next task’s preconditions. If the final result fails, the harness traces backward to the first stage whose outputs stopped tying out.

When a check passes but a downstream step still fails, we learn that the check was too weak. A human tightens it, ratifies the change, and the harness stores the improved verifier for future tasks of the same shape.

This is how the loop learns. It does not become better by trusting the model’s confidence or by asking one probabilistic model to grade another's output. It improves by accumulating a library of human-ratified, deterministic verifiers and strengthening them when failures reveal missing invariants.

Verification produces the fact, and authorization consumes it.

Do not promote the model. Promote the loop, and let the loop learn.

posts.content:
Today, Off-by-1 Labs, 1Password’s security research team, is releasing new research into what happens when AI is asked not just to find vulnerabilities, but to fix them.

Across six recently disclosed, complex vulnerabilities, we generated 6,480 patches using two frontier AI models. The results reveal a critical gap between generating a patch and producing one that is actually safe:
▶️ Just 26.0% fully resolved the vulnerability without materially changing application behavior
▶️ 20.1% fixed the vulnerability but changed how the application worked
▶️ 53.9% failed to resolve the vulnerability, introduced a new vulnerability, or did both

We call them FLAWED: Fix-Like Artifacts with Embedded Defects.

As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, defenders need equally rigorous ways to verify the patches AI produces. Our research shows that expert human review and execution-grounded testing remain essential.

We’re releasing the full research paper, dataset, and open-source tooling to help security teams evaluate AI-generated patching against their own codebases.

Explore the research: https://bit.ly/4xrsUMM

posts.content:
It’s day two at Black Hat and one message is coming through loud and clear. Access is getting more complex and critical.

At the 1Password booth, the conversation revolved around two pressing challenges:

🔐 Reducing standing privilege and securing access to critical systems through just-enough, just-in-time access.
💰 Gaining visibility into rapidly growing AI costs and finding ways to control runaway AI spend.

These themes also surfaced during a panel discussion we hosted with Felicis, Runlayer, and Code Red Partners. Nancy Wang (1Password CTO) opened the session and Jake Storm (Felicis General Partner) moderated the conversation. 

The panel featured Jacob DePriest (1Password CISO) alongside Drew Hintz (OpenAI Product Security Lead), Jonathan Aluveaux (Legora CIO), and Kyle Polley (Perplexity CISO) and explored how organizations can experiment with AI while keeping agents separated from sensitive systems and customer data. Speakers also examined the need for strong observability, audit logs, and consistent controls across an organization’s growing fleet of agents.

As agents take on more work, they should not automatically inherit all of a human’s permissions. Instead, they should request the specific access needed for a task, receive it for a limited period of time, and leave behind a clear record of what they did and why.

AI adoption is moving fast and security teams need an access model that can keep pace without slowing down productivity.

Your business runs on credentials IT did not provision.

A vendor login may sit in an employee’s personal vault even though the person who created it has left the company. The password has never been rotated, and IT may not know the account exists. Yet that credential can still provide access to a critical business system.

The same issue appears across organizations. The contractor logins that outlast the contract, the break-glass accounts copied into multiple vaults, the credentials for apps that do not support SAML or OIDC. They were created outside standard provisioning workflows, but still grant access to real systems.

Earlier this week, we launched 1Password Credential Governance, giving IT and security teams a repeatable workflow to:

🔍 Discover: Find company-owned Login items across employee and shared vaults, filter by domain, and surface high-risk credentials.
🔄 Reclaim: Convert unmanaged credentials into company-managed items, remove duplicates, and reassign access to the right users and teams.
🔐 Govern: Control who can view, use, and edit each credential, rotate or revoke access instantly, and maintain a full audit history of changes.

The result is a continuous record of who can access a credential today and who could access it in the past: https://bit.ly/4fENH8c

#CredentialGovernance #IdentitySecurity #1Password

We are live at #BlackHat2026 🙌

Stop by 📍 Booth 4735 to explore how 1Password helps teams discover, secure, and audit access across human, agent, and machine identities.

Play our Credential Sprawl Capture the Flag 🚩 for a chance to win prizes and earn a spot on our leaderboard.

Today, 1Password CEO David Faugno joined Anthropic CISO Vitaly Gudanets for a fireside chat about what changes when AI agents act across systems.

Capability is not authority. Before an agent acts, can it provide a machine-readable “bill of intent?” The agent identifies the task, the authority it is using, the resources it needs, and the duration of access.

A PAM system could evaluate that intent against policy and provision exactly the authorization required. If the agent’s plan or context changes, the PAM should reevaluate that authorization.

The model determines how to perform the work, the security system determines what the agent is allowed to do.

Our lineup of expert-led sessions this week dives into the identity security gaps that matter: exposed secrets on developer machines, how to eliminate standing access for humans and AI agents, and how to govern AI token spend and consumption.

AI agent adoption is outpacing enterprise governance.

New research finding from the 1Password AI Agent Governance Survey, reveals a widening gap between how quickly agents are entering production and how securely their access is being managed:

🔹 65% of developers are expected or encouraged to use AI agents, but only 33% say they have a highly secure way to do so.
🔹 71% of respondents say agents can access sensitive customer data, intellectual property, or HR information.
🔹 40% of developers give agents persistent access to systems or credentials.
🔹 47% have had an agent take an unintended action after following instructions embedded in untrusted content.

Traditional identity systems were built for a world in which humans initiate logins and access is provisioned at human speed. Agents operate differently: they move across systems, use a combination of human and machine credentials, and can retain access long after a task is complete.
